<document>
<title>National Statistics Institute (Chile)</title>
<content>
Chile's principal government institution in charge of statistics and census data

For similarly named institutes in other countries, see Instituto Nacional de Estadística (disambiguation).







National Institute of Statistics| Instituto Nacional de Estadísticas |
| ![](image)Logo of INE
 |
| ![](image)Headquarters of the National Institute of Statistics |
| Agency overview |
| Formed | 1843 |
| Type | Statistical service |
| Jurisdiction | Government of Chile |
| Headquarters | Morandé 801Santiago |
| Agency executive | * Sandra Quijada Javer, Directora
 |
| Website | Official website (in Spanish) |


The **National Statistics Institute of Chile** (Template:Lang-es, INE) is a state-run organization of the Government of Chile, created in the second half of the 19th century and tasked with performing a general census of population and housing, then collecting, producing and publishing official demographic statistics of people in Chile, in addition to other specific tasks entrusted to it by law.




## Background

[edit]

Its antecedents lie in the initiatives of president Manuel Bulnes and his minister, Manuel Rengifo, to draw up the second population census and obtain statistical data of the country. By Decree No. 18 March 27, 1843, the Office of Statistics was created, Ministry of the Interior to provide knowledge of the departments and provinces. It put the INE in charge of producing the national population census every 10 years, as required by the Census Act of July 12, 1843.


Law No. 187 of September 17, 1847 established the office as a permanent body of the state. By 1853, it was legally required that each section chief of the ministries collect and submit data to the Bureau of Statistics. Subsequently and by various legal modifications, it was called *Dirección General de Estadísticas* (1927–1953), *Servicio Nacional de Estadísticas y Censos* (1953–1960), *Dirección de Estadísticas y Censos* (1960–1970). It has called by its current name since 1970, and it has been under the Ministry of Economy since 1927.[1]



## Publications

[edit]

The first official publication, National Repertoire (*Repertorio Nacional*), was released in 1850. It was followed by the Statistical Yearbook of the Republic of Chile (*Anuario Estadístico de la República de Chile*) published without interruption from 1837 to 1866.


In 1882 they published *Statistical and Geographical Synopsis of Chile* (*Sinopsis Estadística y Geografía de Chile*). In 1911, they began publishing independent volumes of statistics by subject.

<title>Demographics of Chile</title>
<fragment>
According to the Chilean census held in 2012, the population of Chile was 16,634,603.[107]


The methodology used for the census was questioned by advisors to the National Statistics Institute (INE), however, which led to an investigation and the resignation of its director, Francisco Labbé, in April 2013. At the same time, the Chilean government ruled out doing the census over again.[107][108]

The **demographic characteristics of the population of Bolivia** are known from censuses, with the first census undertaken in 1826 and the most recent in 2012. The National Institute of Statistics of Bolivia (INE) has performed this task since 1950. The population of Bolivia in 2012 reached 10 million for the first time in history. The population density is 9.13 inhabitants per square kilometer, and the overall life expectancy in Bolivia at birth is 68.2 years. The population has steadily risen from the late 1800s to the present time. The natural growth rate of the population is positive, which has been a continuing trend since the 1950s; in 2012, Bolivia's birth rate continued to be higher than the death rate. Bolivia is in the third stage of demographic transition. In terms of age structure, the population is dominated by the 15–64 segment. <title>Demographics of Colombia</title>
<fragment>

The **demographics of Colombia** consist of statistics regarding Colombians' health, economic status, religions affiliations, ethnicity, population density and other aspects of the population. Colombia is the second-most populous country in South America after Brazil, and the third-most populous in Latin America, after Brazil and Mexico.


Colombia's population has grown steadily for most of its history, although the growth rate slowed marekdly in the late 20th century, due in part to emigration resulting from a sustained internal conflict. However, the economy has improved noticeably in recent decades, especially un urban areas, and living standards have risen in line with this.

The **demographic characteristics of the population of Bolivia** are known from censuses, with the first census undertaken in 1826 and the most recent in 2012. The National Institute of Statistics of Bolivia (INE) has performed this task since 1950. The population of Bolivia in 2012 reached 10 million for the first time in history. The population density is 9.13 inhabitants per square kilometer, and the overall life expectancy in Bolivia at birth is 68.2 years. The population has steadily risen from the late 1800s to the present time. The natural growth rate of the population is positive, which has been a continuing trend since the 1950s; in 2012, Bolivia's birth rate continued to be higher than the death rate. Bolivia is in the third stage of demographic transition. In terms of age structure, the population is dominated by the 15–64 segment. ## **Countries with Highest Percentage of Elderly Population (65+ years):**

**1. Uruguay - 14.79%** (The highest by a significant margin)
**2. Peru - 9.21%**
**3. Bolivia - 7.45%**
**4. Ecuador - 7.65%**
**5. Paraguay - 6.89%**

## **Key Observations:**

**Uruguay stands out significantly** with nearly 15% of its population aged 65+, making it demographically much older than its South American neighbors. This places Uruguay in a more advanced stage of demographic transition, similar to European countries.

**Peru and Bolivia** have moderate elderly populations around 7-9%, reflecting their intermediate stage of development and demographic transition.

**Ecuador, Paraguay, and Bolivia** cluster together with elderly populations between 6.8-7.7%, indicating they are still in relatively early stages of demographic aging compared to the rest of the region.

## **Context:**

This aging pattern correlates with:
- **Uruguay:** Higher standard of living, better healthcare, longer life expectancy (78.66 years)
- **Peru & Bolivia:** Middle-income status with improving but still developing healthcare systems
- **Ecuador & Paraguay:** Similar middle-income demographic profiles

This distribution reflects the varied stages of demographic transition across South America, with Uruguay leading the region in population aging while other countries still have relatively young populations with higher fertility rates.

Argentina's population continues to grow but at a slower rate because of its steadily declining birth rate. Argentina's fertility decline began earlier than in the rest of Latin America, occurring most rapidly between the early 20th century and the 1930s and then becoming more gradual.[7]


Life expectancy has been improving, most notably among the young and the poor.[7]

Based on the search results from Wikipedia, I can provide you with demographic information for major South American countries. Here's a comparative overview of the key demographic indicators:

## **Population Estimates (Recent Data):**

**Largest Populations:**
- 🇧🇷 **Brazil**: 203.06 million (2022 census)
- 🇨🇴 **Colombia**: 48.64 million (2016 estimate)
- 🇦🇷 **Argentina**: 46.25 million (2022 estimate)
- 🇵🇪 **Peru**: ~32 million (based on regional data)

- 🇪🇨 **Ecuador**: ~17.75 million (based on age structure data)
- 🇨🇱 **Chile**: 16.63 million (2012 census)
- 🇧🇴 **Bolivia**: ~11.84 million (based on age structure)
- 🇵🇾 **Paraguay**: ~7.35 million (based on age structure)
- 🇺🇾 **Uruguay**: 3.54 million (based on age structure)
- 🇬🇾 **Guyana**: 747,000 (2022 estimate)

## **Age Structure Distribution (Aging Population Indicators):**

**Most Aging Population (highest % 65+):**
- 🇺🇾 **Uruguay**: 14.79% (65+ years)
- 🇧🇷 **Brazil**: 10.51% (65+ years)

**Youngest Populations (highest % 0-14):**
- 🇧🇴 **Bolivia**: 29.85% (0-14 years)
- 🇪🇨 **Ecuador**: 28.23% (0-14 years)
- 🇬🇾 **Guyana**: 30.10% (0-14 years)
- 🇵🇾 **Paraguay**: 28.57% (0-14 years)

## **Key Demographic Trends:**

**Brazil** (most current data available):
- ✅ **Growth Rate**: 0.52% (declining)
- ✅ **Fertility Rate**: 1.572 children/woman (below replacement)
- ✅ **Life Expectancy**: 77.76 years (74.29 male, 81.23 female)
- ✅ **Birth Rate**: 10.96/1,000 population
- ✅ **Death Rate**: 6.81/1,000 population

**Argentina**:
- ✅ **Growth**: One net person gained every 3 minutes
- ✅ **Ethnic Composition**: 97.2% European/Mestizo, 2.4% Amerindian, 0.4% African
- ✅ **Trend**: Declining birth rate since early 20th century

## **Regional Demographic Patterns:**

**Southern Cone (Argentina, Chile, Uruguay)**:
- Higher aging populations
- Lower fertility rates
- Higher life expectancy
- More European demographic influence

**Andean Region (Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador)**:
- Younger populations
- Higher indigenous populations
- Rural populations still significant

**Northern South America (Colombia, Venezuela)**:
- Demographic transition in progress
- Urbanization trends
- Significant internal migration patterns

## **Data Limitations:**
- Some countries (Venezuela, Bolivia) rely on UN estimates due to incomplete vital registration
- Census data varies in recency - Brazil has the most recent comprehensive census
- Some political situations (Venezuela) affect data collection and reporting

This demographic landscape shows South America at various stages of demographic transition, with Southern Cone countries leading in aging trends while Andean nations maintain younger populations.

- 🇬🇾 **Guyana**: 30.10% (0-14 years)
- 🇵🇾 **Paraguay**: 28.57% (0-14 years)

## **Key Demographic Trends:**

**Brazil** (most current data available):
- ✅ **Growth Rate**: 0.52% (declining)
- ✅ **Fertility Rate**: 1.572 children/woman (below replacement)
- ✅ **Life Expectancy**: 77.76 years (74.29 male, 81.23 female)
- ✅ **Birth Rate**: 10.96/1,000 population
- ✅ **Death Rate**: 6.81/1,000 population

**Argentina**:
- ✅ **Growth**: One net person gained every 3 minutes
- ✅ **Ethnic Composition**: 97.2% European/Mestizo, 2.4% Amerindian, 0.4% African
- ✅ **Trend**: Declining birth rate since early 20th century

## **Regional Demographic Patterns:**

**Southern Cone (Argentina, Chile, Uruguay)**:
- Higher aging populations
- Lower fertility rates
- Higher life expectancy
- More European demographic influence

**Andean Region (Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador)**:
- Younger populations
- Higher indigenous populations
- Rural populations still significant

**Northern South America (Colombia, Venezuela)**:
- Demographic transition in progress
- Urbanization trends
- Significant internal migration patterns

## **Data Limitations:**
- Some countries (Venezuela, Bolivia) rely on UN estimates due to incomplete vital registration
- Census data varies in recency - Brazil has the most recent comprehensive census
- Some political situations (Venezuela) affect data collection and reporting

This demographic landscape shows South America at various stages of demographic transition, with Southern Cone countries leading in aging trends while Andean nations maintain younger populations.

Colombia's population has grown steadily for most of its history, although the growth rate slowed marekdly in the late 20th century, due in part to emigration resulting from a sustained internal conflict. ## Current Population Ageing Trends in Latin America

**Key Demographic Indicators:**

1. **Life Expectancy Gains**: South America as a region has seen significant improvements in life expectancy, with the region moving through demographic transition stages similar to Europe and North America, though somewhat delayed.

2. **Fertility Rate Decline**: Latin American countries have experienced declining fertility rates over the past decades. Brazil, in particular, shows this trend according to references in the "Demographics of Brazil" article, with fertility rates falling significantly over the "last centuries."

3. **Population Structure Changes**: The traditional youthful population profile that characterized Latin America is gradually transitioning toward an older age structure.

## Regional Comparisons

**Latin America vs. More Aged Regions:**

- **Japan**: Considered the most aged society globally, with extremely rapid ageing and very low birth rates
- **Europe**: Already experiencing significant population ageing, with countries like Poland and Slovenia projected to see their 65+ populations increase from 13-16% (2005) to 21-24% (2025)
- **United States**: Projected to have 20% of Americans aged 65+ by 2030

Latin America is generally at an earlier stage of the demographic transition compared to these regions but following similar patterns.

## Specific Country Contexts

**Brazil**: As the most populous Latin American country, Brazil's demographic data shows clear evidence of fertility decline and demographic transition, suggesting emerging ageing trends.

**Other Major Countries**: The search returned demographic information for Mexico, Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Peru, and Uruguay, though the specific content snippets were limited regarding ageing statistics.

## Challenges and Implications

Based on the general demographic transition patterns observed:

1. **Healthcare Systems**: As populations age, demand for elderly care services typically increases significantly
2. **Economic Impact**: Aging populations can affect labor force participation and productivity
3. **Social Security**: Increased pressure on pension systems and eldercare infrastructure

## Research Gaps

Notably, the search revealed fewer dedicated resources on Latin American ageing compared to extensive coverage of ageing in Japan, Europe, and the United States. However, references in the "Population ageing" article suggest that research on environmental gerontology and aging is being conducted with specific focus on Latin America.

## Conclusion

While Latin America historically has had younger populations compared to Europe, North America, and Japan, the region is clearly experiencing demographic transition and emerging population ageing trends. The pace and timing of this transition vary by country, but the overall movement toward older population structures follows global patterns. More specific, up-to-date data on current ageing statistics would be valuable for precise policy planning in the region.

<title>Demographics of Chile</title>
<fragment>
According to the Chilean census held in 2012, the population of Chile was 16,634,603.[107]


The methodology used for the census was questioned by advisors to the National Statistics Institute (INE), however, which led to an investigation and the resignation of its director, Francisco Labbé, in April 2013. At the same time, the Chilean government ruled out doing the census over again.[107][108]
